memo.intro: First-look memo as of 2026-11-01. Public data only. Every factual sentence links to its source; a separate verifier removed unsupported claims.

sentences.text: The GitHub repository roboninecom/SO-ARM102 describes an open-source SO-ARM102 robot arm, successor to SO-ARM100 and SO-ARM101.
sentences.note: Description states exactly this in source 13.

sentences.text: The repository describes a LeRobot-compatible leader-follower kit for teleoperation and imitation learning, with improved rigidity, a parallel gripper, STEP/STL files and a BOM.
sentences.note: Description lists LeRobot-compatible leader-follower kit, improved rigidity, parallel gripper, STEP/STL files and BOM.

sentences.text: The repository was created on 2026-09-19.
It had 178 stars and 10 forks as of 2026-11-02.
The homepage listed is https://robonine.com.
This looks like an open-hardware project at an early stage, with community activity but no visible commercial detail in the evidence.
We cannot judge founder background, technical depth, or team size from this record.
The repository description says the kit comes with improved rigidity, a parallel gripper, STEP/STL files and a BOM.
sentences.note: Description mentions STEP/STL files and BOM as part of the kit and improved rigidity and parallel gripper, but 'lists' files and 'adds' a gripper go slightly beyond; description says 'with improved rigidity, parallel gripper'. Nothing states it adds a gripper relative to predecessors.

sentences.text: The file tree shows 281 files at commit f7e17fe, including .github/workflows/ci.yaml and docs/i18n README files under language folders such as ar, de, en, es, fr and hi.
sentences.note: 281 files at f7e17fe and ci.yaml are stated; translations appear as docs/i18n paths for ar, de, en, es, fr, hi, which supports several languages, though the paths shown are README files under docs/i18n. Commit hash is f7e17fe33c, fine. Mostly supported, but 'README translations' is an interpretation of paths.

sentences.text: What looks novel is an incremental redesign of an existing open low-cost arm family, aimed at stiffer structure and a better gripper.
What is hard is holding repeatability and backlash low with printed parts and hobby-grade actuators, while keeping the kit cheap and easy to build.
The main technical risk is that the rigidity gains are not measured in public, so the improvement over SO-ARM101 may be hard to prove and easy to copy.
The repository topics include imitation-learning, lerobot, robot-learning and open-hardware.
sentences.note: Topics include imitation-learning, lerobot, open-hardware and robot-learning.

sentences.text: The target buyers appear to be researchers, students and hobbyists doing imitation learning on low-cost arms.
Interest in learned manipulation may be raising demand for cheap data-collection hardware, but the evidence does not size this market.
The repository was created on 2026-09-19.
Pull requests on the page span 2026-10-05 to 2026-11-01, and 36 were listed as of 2026-11-02.
Of those 36 pull requests, 23 were by people outside the owning organization.
sentences.note: 23 of the 36 pull requests by people outside the owning organization.

sentences.text: Three releases were dated 2026-10-07, 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-22.
The 10 forks listed were dated 2026-10-07 to 2026-10-27.
Two issues were listed, dated 2026-10-13 and 2026-10-30, both by people outside the owning organization.
sentences.note: 2 issues dated 2026-10-13 and 2026-10-30, both by outsiders.

The latest push was on 2026-11-02, and the latest commit listed was dated 2026-11-01.

sentences.text: Open hardware can be copied by anyone, so the moat may depend on brand, supply, quality and support rather than the design.
Outside pull requests may include translations or small fixes, so they may not signal deep technical engagement.
Star counts are a weak proxy for sales or real usage.
The arm builds on prior SO-ARM designs and the LeRobot ecosystem, which creates dependence on projects the company does not control.
The public record does not show whether the company sells kits, at what price, or in what volume.
It does not show who the founders are, how the company is funded, or how large the team is.
It does not show benchmark data on rigidity, accuracy or policy success rates against SO-ARM101.
It does not show the license terms or how the company plans to earn revenue from an open design.

founder_call_questions: Who is on the team, and what are your backgrounds in mechanical design and robot learning?
What measurements show the rigidity gain over SO-ARM101, such as deflection, backlash or repeatability?
What does the parallel gripper change in grasp success on real imitation learning tasks?
What is the bill of materials cost and the kit price, and what are gross margins?
How many kits have you sold or shipped, and to which customer types?
What is the business model if the design is open source, and what stops a cheaper copy?
What license covers the hardware files and the software?
How many of the 23 outside pull requests are substantive design or code changes versus translations and docs?
What is your relationship with the LeRobot team and the original SO-ARM authors?
What is your supply chain for actuators and printed parts, and how do you handle quality and lead times?
